newsitem.title: USA: CBOT CORN SEEN SURGING TO $3.00 OR MORE - PANEL.
newsitem.headline: CBOT CORN SEEN SURGING TO $3.00 OR MORE - PANEL.

text.p: The U.S. Department of Agriculture's shockingly low production estimate for 1997 U.S. corn at 9.276 billion bushels was expected to quickly boost Chicago Board of Trade corn futures and eventually the market could rally above $3.00 per bushel, analysts said.

"We're going to have a very electrifying day here at the (Chicago) Board of Trade and I imagine at some time today we'll be limit up," said Dan Basse, executive vice president of Chicago-based analytical firm AgResource, Inc. "The days of $2.50 corn are over."

Basse and Goldenberg Hehmeyer grain/oilseed analyst Bob Lekberg Tuesday addressed the Chicago Board of Trade's media briefing following the 0730 CDT release of USDA's August crop production and supply/demand reports.

USDA said 1997 U.S. corn production would total 9.276 billion bushels, well below an average of analysts' estimates for 9.554 billion, sharply below the government's July forecast for 9.7 billion and was below the lowest analyst forecast for 9.375 billion bushels.
As a result, some analysts expected CBOT corn Tuesday to open up the 12-cent-per-bushel daily trading limit.
The September contract Monday closed at $2.49-3/4 per bushel.
Basse said "the corn market ultimately could go to $3.00 to $3.50 per bushel."
Lekberg said the CBOT corn futures could go to $3.25 per bushel.
USDA cut to 847 million bushels its forecast for 1997-97 (September-August) U.S. corn ending stocks from the July forecast for 941 million bushels.
The panel members agreed the fate of U.S. corn prices also hinges on how quickly world importers come into the U.S. market for purchase of their feed needs.
"The near-term price depends on how soon we can get world buyers in," Basse said.
Basse and Lekberg cited China again as a wild card in the U.S. corn export picture.
USDA cut its estimate of China corn exports in half to one million tonnes and reduced China's corn production by 12 million tonnes to 110 million tonnes due to drought.
"For China corn, 110 million tonnes is a good guess," Lekberg said.
"It's the year of the grains. Last year was the year of the oilseeds with beans going to $9.00 per bushel," Basse said.
The CBOT nearby soybean contract in mid-May, surged to a high of $9.03-1/2 per bushel on tight supplies of U.S. soybeans.
USDA pegged 1997 U.S. soybean production at a record 2.744 billion bushels, above an average of analysts' estimates for 2.680 billion.
"The soybean number is larger than expected but this is only a benchmark," Basse said. The August USDA soybean survey is based on a count of soybean plants and is not a count of soybean pods.
"The crop can still go either way," Lekberg said.
"I would said the USDA's figure of 2.744 is at the upper extreme of soy production potential," Basse said.
The government also surprised the market Tuesday by hiking its estimate for 1997 U.S. wheat production to 2.531 billion bushels, above an average of analysts' estimates for 2.476 billion.

"The all wheat production was a bearish number and the market should be a little lower," Basse said of opening CBOT soft red winter wheat futures. But the expected rally in corn could turn wheat higher, Basse said.
"I think the corn will bolster wheat," Lekberg said.

USDA boosted its winter wheat production forecast to 1.855 billion bushels from the previous 1.781 billion and spring wheat was raised to 585 million bushels from USDA's previous estimate of 569 million.
